#3384. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3383. Democrat Annie Andrews Upsets Darline Graham to Win South Carolina Senate Seat

In a shocking upset, pediatrician Annie Andrews has claimed the South Carolina Senate seat once occupied by the late, staunch Trump ally Lindsey Graham — and, before him, the infamous segregationist Strom Thurmond. The seat has not been held by a Democrat since 1964.

“South Carolina, you have shown the nation — in an era of partisan divides, of vitriol and namecalling, in a politics dominated by billionaires, special interests, and insiders in Washington — that we will not bow down,” Andrews wrote shortly after the race was called. “We will not back down. And we will chart our own course.”

Andrews declared her candidacy in 2025, motivated, she’s said, by Trump’s nomination of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who she named her “professional arch-nemesis,” to lead the Department of Health and Human Services.

She had already been running against Lindsey Graham for more than a year when he died unexpectedly in July. His sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his seat, and later won the GOP nomination.

Graham mounted a campaign seeking to capitalize on her political inexperience, declaring, for instance, “I don’t speak politician,” and famously admitting, on the primary debate stage that she was “not that informed on national security … national security is not my thing.”

Andrews, like other Democrats across the nation, remained laser-focused on cost of living and quality of life issues like healthcare, data centers, and the price of diesel.

Speaking to Rolling Stone earlier this year, Andrews emphasized her focus on healthcare, data centers, and the price of diesel. ”I’m in this race because of my experience working within America’s broken healthcare system,” she said. “I started to realize what I was seeing from hospital room to hospital room were the impacts of broken policies coming from Washington, harming my patients and their families.” Trending Stories Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and 'You Can See Everything' Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

Andrews also spoke of the potential to collaborate with her GOP colleagues, particularly on data centers. “Republicans and Democrats are completely united in their opposition to this unchecked data center development in our rural communities. It’s not just one part of the state where we’ve had these conversations. It’s community after community after community,” she said. “These companies swoop in to these rural communities, dangle a few carrots in front of local elected officials, and then these communities get steamrolled and they’re not getting transparency about the economic impact or the environmental impact, and then these huge facilities are just being built in their backyard.”

Her victory on Tuesday — one of a slough of Democratic wins — brings to mind the words of her late opponent, Lindsey Graham, when Donald Trump was running for the Republican nomination for president in 2016. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed,” Graham wrote. “And we will deserve it.”

#3382. John Ternus addresses iPhone Duo supply constraints, display issue

Today Apple reported record Q4 earnings, which beat Wall Street expectations overall. And in an interview with Reuters, CEO John Ternus addressed current iPhone Duo supply constraints and also referenced units that have been returned for display issues.

Apple’s latest quarterly earnings did not include any sales for the iPhone Duo. That’s because it covered a period running July-September, and the Duo didn’t go on sale until October.

But Wall Street is understandably still very curious about how sales for the foldable are going. Especially as relates to revenue forecasts for the current quarter.

In an interview with Reuters, Ternus addressed two aspects of the iPhone Duo: supply constraints and units that have had display issues.

Regarding supply, it sounds like Apple doesn’t know when it might reach supply-demand balance:

“Duo is constrained as of today,” Ternus said. “The ramp is going well, and we’re working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we’re not ‌able to ⁠predict when supply and demand will be in balance.”

Currently, shipping estimates from the Apple Store are still set for late January. That’s where they’ve stayed since the first pre-orders immediately sold out on October 16.

On the matter of iPhone Duo screens cracking, Ternus was brief and essentially repeated what Apple had previously confirmed: that the issue is real, but limited to a very small number of units.

Ternus told Reuters that “a very small percentage” of iPhone Duo units had been returned with display issues. Apple is replacing those units with new models.

#3380. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3379. Texas Goes Blue: James Talarico Triumphs Over Ken Paxton

The myth of a blue Texas is now a reality.

Democrat James Talarico has defeated Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the year. Shortly after Talarico was projected to win, Democrat Gina Hinojosa was projected the winner over longtime Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

The victories marks a seismic shift in Texas politics, and in the nation’s current political map, ending a 32-year statewide drought for Democrats in the Republican stronghold. The party now controls the state’s governership, as well as a U.S. Senate seat there for at least the next six years.

The Senate race started with two bitter primaries, with Talarico defeating Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) on the Democratic side, and Paxton defeating incumbent Senator John Cornyn after landing Donald Trump’s endorsement. Cornyn refused to endorse his party’s nominee after losing the primary, citing Paxton’s long record of corruption and abuse of office. In audio leaked to Rolling Stone last month, Paxton griped about how much the contentious primary with Paxton hurt his chances.

Cornyn was one of the first to celebrate Talarico’s win on Tuesday. “The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate,” he wrote. “I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Throughout most of the general election campaign, Talarico held a polling lead over Paxton. The upstart candidate barnstormed the state for months before Paxton even began to put on his campaigning shoes. Talarico, a state House member, ran on an economically progressive platform focused on cost of living issues and anti-corruption. Paxton, a poster boy for corruption, ran largely on his allegiance to Trump while trying to paint Talarico as a radical leftist.

Talarico sought to take advantage of a uniquely abysmal landscape for Republicans across the country to steal a seat for Democrats in a state that voted for Trump by a 13-point margin in 2024. Trump, ironically enough, turned out to be Talarico’s biggest campaign asset. The president’s approval numbers tanked when he launched his war against Iran this spring — breaking his “no more wars” campaign promise and sending the price of fuel skyrocketing. It hasn’t exactly been a winning strategy. Inflation is up, wage growth is stagnant, and Americans can’t afford the life their parents had. At the same time, Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire dumped almost half a billion dollars into Republican reelection efforts — much of it into Texas.Paxton, like many Texas Republicans, spent the campaign operating under the assumption that just being the GOP nominee would be enough to notch a win. Paxton ducked the three proposed network debates between himself and Talarico, studiously avoided interactions with any press not explicitly aligned with the right, and struggled to develop any level of compelling personal charm over the course of the race.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Trump’s support of Paxton — over an incumbent Republican and the objections of Senate GOP leaders —  elevated the Texas race into a referendum on Trumpism writ large. The president campaigned throughout the state alongside Paxton, including hosting an “emergency” midterm republican convention in Dallas, Texas. Paxton was then caught complaining in leaked audio that the president’s appearance had hurt his numbers. Unable to distance himself from the president, Paxton and his allies attempted to reframe the race towards culture war fear mongering. Hundreds of millions were deployed in ad spending — including $158 million from Elon Musk — attempting to link Talarico to trangender issues, immigration anarchy, and (it really only works in Texas) accusations of veganism.  Related Content Mastodon Seek Partial Dismissal of Brent Hinds Estate's Lawsuit Against Them Tinashe to Republican Voters During Midterm Elections: 'Yall Can Go' Can Dems Actually Win the Senate? Here’s How the Key Races Are Breaking How to Livestream Midterm Election-Night News for Free Without Cable

Despite the monetary advantages held by the GOP, Trump has shed basically all the support he managed to accumulate among disaffected Hispanic voters during the 2024 election — a critical constituency within Texas. Early voting data indicated that enthusiasm among Republican voters was trailing Democrats.

The candidates spent the final hours of the campaign making last-second pitches to voters, offering vastly competing visions for the state and nation.

At a Monday concert rally in the heart of Austin, Talarico and Hinojosa spoke before a full house crowd of almost 2,000 people. Talarico, swimming against a three-decade long tide of GOP rule in the state, reminded his supporters of the Texas of yore — and the Democrats who shaped it.

“We are the state that pioneered ranching and energy and computers. We are the state that gave this country Barbara Jordan, Anne Richards, LBJ and the great society,” Talarico said. “We are the state that put breakfast in a taco. There is nothing we can’t do.”

The Democrat contrasted his vision of the state with the governance of state and federal Republican leadership. “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Talarico said, repeatedly referencing Ken Paxton’s extensive record of profiteering and abuse of office. “This election should be about chasing a vision of what this state can be. Texas public schools that are the envy of the nation. A Texas economy that is second to none and Texas families that are stronger and healthier than they have ever been before. This won’t happen overnight, but a giant state deserves giant dreams.”

Paxton was originally scheduled to close his “Come and Take It” campaign tour with a large rally at The Alamo — a historic landmark of the Texas Revolution famously taken by the Mexican force. Paxton cancelled the rally and instead shifted his event to Allen, Texas, in the suburbs of Dallas.

The state attorney general’s closing pitch to voters was decidedly less rosy. In front of a much smaller crowd, Paxton warned of the threats of socialism, transgender inclusive healthcare, men in women’s sports, unfettered mass immigration, and a whole host of culture war priorities that had so far failed to secure him a major lead in the polls.  Trending Stories Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and 'You Can See Everything' Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

“We are all sinners and we all need you,” Paxton told supporters in a prayer ahead of his speech.

In the end, not enough Texans bought Paxton’s pitch.

#3378. Apple spent a record $45.77 billion on R&D in fiscal 2026, up 32%

Apple’s research and development expenses reached a new all-time high in fiscal 2026, climbing 32% year over year to $45.77 billion. Here are the details.

While it may have taken Apple longer than some wished it had to ramp up R&D in the face of growing competition in AI, the company has significantly accelerated its spending over the past year.

As Apple shared in its Q4 2026 results, it spent $11.73 billion on R&D, bringing its total spending for fiscal 2026 to $45.77 billion, a 32% increase compared to the $34.55 billion it spent in fiscal 2025.

During an earnings call earlier this year, former CEO Tim Cook said Apple was “clearly investing more,” adding that R&D was “accelerating much higher than the company” overall. CFO Kevan Parekh also explained that AI-related spending was being added to the investments Apple was already making in its existing product roadmap.

Interestingly, today’s figures also suggest that Apple’s R&D spending may be starting to level off.

While Apple’s Q4 2026 R&D expenses were up 32% from $8.87 billion in the year-ago quarter, they were virtually unchanged from Q3, increasing by just $1 million. As the chart above shows, Apple’s R&D spending jumped significantly at the beginning of fiscal 2026, but has since stabilized at a much higher level than in previous years.

#3377. Modern Warfare 4 is the shooter you've been waiting for if you skipped the last few Call of Duty games

While none of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s three modes are perfect, they’re all solid enough to deliver a well-rounded experience anchored by the franchise's incredible gunplay.

DMZ mode is solid and has potential to get better

DMZ mode is a little more PVP than I’d like

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Platforms: Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S (reviewed)Price: $69 / £69 / AU$109Release Date: October 23, 2026Genre: First-person shooter

The Call of Duty season has arrived, and this year Infinity Ward is back in the driver’s seat. After back-to-back Black Ops games, Activision’s FPS cash cow returns to the Modern Warfare moniker and gameplay style, which I've always preferred (not that I dislike Black Ops; I just prefer MW's cast of characters and gameplay).

Modern Warfare 4 feels like a return to form for the long-running franchise, both in the single-player campaign and in the overall gunplay. The time-to-kill is a little longer than in the last couple of games, letting you use more inventive tactics in firefights. It’s not just about who shot who first. And I’m genuinely torn. It doesn’t feel like what I’m used to from the franchise, but maybe that’s not such a bad thing.

If you never liked COD games, nothing here will change your mind, but if you’re a lapsed fan of the series who wants to see how Captain Price’s story ties up and still enjoy a fun first-person shooter, this might be the one to come back to.

I'm generally not a Call of Duty campaign fan. I usually play a few hours a year and spend the rest of the time longing for multiplayer, so I fizzle out about halfway through. Which is why I was shocked when the Modern Warfare 4 campaign actually hooked me right off the bat and kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through.

Sure, the story is a little convoluted, especially the Price portion, which has the unenviable task of cleaning up the mess left by the last few Call of Duty: Modern Warfare games. But I think it does a fantastic job of tying up all the loose ends into a coherent story that successfully caps Price’s story (at least until the next time Modern Warfare gets rebooted).

Price’s missions take place five days before the story’s other half (you’re essentially playing two campaigns at once and switching back and forth). His story crescendos with the start of the other plot and a massive Korean invasion.

Price’s story will make you feel like Jason Statham or John Wick, running around shooting and fighting in first-person hand-to-hand combat. The Korean story has a more traditional war-game feel and follows Park Hyun Jun and his squad. They’re entertaining, with a mix of Korean and US soldiers who add lighthearted humor during intense frontline moments.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The two interwoven stories contrast in a way that makes this the best Call of Duty campaign since 2009’s Modern Warfare 2.

Both sides of the campaign can get a little dark and heavy. An early scene puts you in the shoes of an invader on the Korean side, forcing difficult decisions that can make you wonder if you're the hero or villain (or somewhere in the gray middle ground). For example, an early Price fight scene ends in pure and utter brutality.

Then there’s the heavily hyped Stranded mission, a ramped-up version of the DMZ mode with a story and characters you actually care about. While most of the campaign is linear, this mission gives you a level of freedom we don’t often see in COD games. It’s dripping with tension and best of all, it’s fun. It was a dangerous call for Infinity Ward to include one mission that stands out, as it risked making the rest of the campaign feel inferior. However, because the more traditional COD missions are also so well executed and the stakes feel so high, this problem is negated.

I got seriously into Arc Raiders for about a month before some updates made me fall off. It was my first taste of an extraction shooter, and it felt good to return to the genre with DMZ mode. It’s definitely the weakest of the three main modes in Modern Warfare 4, but it’s still fun.

We already know the extraction formula is successful. In my opinion, Call of Duty is the best first-person shooter franchise from a pure gunplay perspective, so it makes sense that smooshing the two together would lead to a solid online mode.

The missions in DMZ are relatively generic and basic, but they’re motivation enough to keep you moving through a session beyond just grabbing the best loot and extracting.

My only issue with DMZ comes from the overall COD culture. Years of competitive multiplayer have created a shoot-first mentality that removes much of the tension that comes from talking to people in other extraction shooters. I love the “hey, are you cool?” interactions I experienced in Arc Raiders (and even in the Dark Zone of The Division), and in the DMZ matches I played for this review, every encounter with other players was instantly hostile.

The thrill of finding loot and getting out at an extraction point is as satisfying as any other game in the genre (perhaps even more so, because getting your loot almost certainly involved fighting another player who attacked as you tried to extract).

And while there wasn’t much in the way of enemy negotiations, I had great experiences with other players in my squad. In almost every match, my random squadmates cared as much about my survival and successful extraction as I did.

I look forward to seeing how Infinity Ward builds on DMZ, both in this Modern Warfare 4 and across future COD titles.

For me, this is the main event of any Call of Duty game. Sure, the campaign is fun for eight hours or so, and other modes like Black Ops’ Zombies and DMZ will hook a certain percentage of the player base; it’s multiplayer that has made this franchise one of the biggest in gaming history.

And while it had a few small flaws at launch (erratic spawns and skill-based matchmaking being all over the place with so many new players), the overall experience is there, and it’s great. The guns are fun to level up and add new attachments (the usual slots are all there), and it even adds new modes that borrow from other FPS games, like Collateral, a round-based plant-and-defuse mode with buy stages like Counter-Strike. It’s a well-executed game mode that feels fresh even if it’s been done before outside of COD.

Frontline is a spawn-campers' dream. Instead of spawning in logical, somewhat “safe” locations, you only spawn in your base. This becomes a problem when you’re on the losing team, because the other squad knows exactly where you’ll pop up next. Sure, you get a couple of seconds of invincibility, but that’s hardly enough to save this mode.

Map selection will always be contentious when a Call of Duty game launches. Some players will call them inventive and fun while others will say they’re more of the same. I'm in the latter camp, as the only map that does anything exciting is Kill Block, with its shifting, evolving nature. Sadly, that’s only available as a 10 vs. 10 map, so traditional 6 vs. 6 players won’t even see it.

However, even if no map in the normal rotation stands out as exceptionally good, none stand out as outright bad. Each map is good enough to have fun shooting enemies across, and that’s really all I’m looking for (though, like most COD launches, spawn points need a tweak, as I’ve had a few times where I died and spawned right in an enemy’s field of view). Hopefully this will be one of the first things IW fixes with the inevitable post-launch patches.

My favorite mode has always been, and always will be, Team Deathmatch. There’s something pure about two teams of six going head-to-head to see who can eliminate the other side more. But I’ve also enjoyed some Domination, another staple of the COD games. Fortunately, Infinity Ward kept these and all the other staples intact for Modern Warfare 4 (Kill Confirmed, Search and Destroy, Hardpoint, etc.). If you’re coming into this game looking for the stuff you already know you love, I can assure you it’s all there and just as good as ever.

I love Modern Warfare 4. I’m confident I’ll keep playing this version of Call of Duty through the rest of 2026 and deep into 2027, until the next game in the annualized series drops (with a break to follow soon for Grand Theft Auto VI).

Infinity Ward has reminded everyone that it is the “A” developer of Call of Duty, and Modern Warfare 4 will be a tough act for Raven, Treyarch and Sledgehammer to follow. All three modes are fun, and the campaign sucked me in and kept me playing, as none have since the original Modern Warfare 2 (which I still stand by as the best COD campaign ever released). I’d go so far as to say this is in the top three COD campaigns of all time.

Add in the multiplayer and the extraction-based DMZ mode, and you have a well-rounded Call of Duty package that will please fans. It probably won’t convince people who already don’t like COD, but lapsed fans and hardcore players will find plenty to keep them coming back again and again.

#3376. ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover’ Wins Grand Prix At Tokyo International Film Festival

Sister Brother Manhole Cover, from Macedonian filmmaker Milcho Manchevski, won the the top award at this year’s Tokyo International Film Festival.

The film was presented with the Tokyo Grand Prix/The Governor of Tokyo Award, which comes with a cash prize of $19,000 (JYP3M). One of 15 films in Tokyo’s main competition section, it follows a pair of siblings in post-Communist Macedonia, who make their living stealing bronze busts and manhole covers, until an injury forces them into contact with the Macedonian underworld. (You can read Deadline’s interview with the filmmaker here.) Related Stories News Teodora Ana Mihai On Her Breakout Feature 'Heysel 85' & Plans For Her Next Film -- Tokyo News Japan's Animation Industry Grows 15.8% To Record $28BN, Driven By Both Domestic & Overseas Sales - TIFFCOM

Sun Xun’s Magic Atlas, an animated feature from Singapore, was presented with the festival’s Special Jury Prize and a cash award of JPY500,000 ($3,160). Chinese artist Sun Xun spent ten years making the film, which combines animation with ink wash painting, medieval European engravings and other styles of art. Watch on Deadline

The Award for Best Director went to Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso for Double Freedom, about a solitary woodcutter who is faced with taking in his sister when the mental institution she lives in closes. Best Actress went to Hu Ling for The Night That Binds Us, A France-Hong Kong production directed by Wang Jiangyong, while Japan’s Narita Ryo won Best Actor for Two Cigarettes, Three Nights, directed by Mishima Yukiko.

The Award for Best Artistic Contribution was presented to Until The Day Ends from Serbian filmmaker Jelena Maksimović. The Audience Award went to Heysel 85, directed by Romanian filmmaker Teodora Ana Mihai (read Deadline’s interview with the director here). The awards for Best Director, Actor, Actress and Best Artistic Contribution all came with a cash prize of $1,900 (JPY300,000).

Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer headed the main competition jury, which also included Tokyo and New York-based producer Alex Lo, Korean producer Oh Jungwan, French colorist Yov Moor and Japanese actress Makiko Watanabe.

In the Asian Future competition for emerging Asian filmmakers, Best Film with a cash prize of JPY1M ($6,320) was presented to Serife Tavsan, directed by Afghan filmmaker Tareq Daoud. The Asian Future Special Mention went to Indonesian drama Jani Be Good, directed by Ariani Darmawan.

The Asian Future Jury included Japanese producer Eiko Mizuno-Gray, Japanese filmmaker Akio Fujimoto and Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara.

Nippon Cinema Now, the festival’s section that presents a showcase of contemporary Japanese cinema, also handed out two prizes, which were introduced for the first time this year. The Best Film Award (JPY500,000) was presented to Silver Express, directed by Tanaka Miki, while the Special Jury Prize (JPY300,000) went to Between Us from Matsumura Shingo.

In the Asian Students’ Film Conference, the Best Film Award (JPY300,000) went to Running Wild In The Sun, while the Special Jury Prize was jointly awarded to Everything’s Peachy and All Of Her, which received JPY100,000 each.

The TIFF Ethical Film Award (JPY200,000), which had a separate jury headed by actor Isomura Hayato, went to Isabelle Stever’s I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming. The award aims to raise awareness of social issues including the environment, poverty and discrimination.

As previously announced, the Kurosawa Akira Award went to Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof and Japanese filmmaker Mipo O. Tokyo International Film Festival ran from October 26 to November 4, 2026.

#3375. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3373. Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout

When things go wrong, we look to our leaders for answers. And in what appears to be a historic wipeout for Donald Trump’s Republican party, the President has a clear idea of what went wrong: his idiot lackeys failed him.

Republican candidates faced a brutal national climate in the 2026 midterms. Donald Trump’s war in Iran, harsh tariff policy, and overall instability had rocked the global economy, making gas and consumer goods prices skyrocket, cratering his own popularity. Candidates who had spent years fighting for his favor now found themselves desperately trying to distance themselves in the eyes of voters. But in Trump’s opinion, none of that was his fault. In fact, it’s the candidates who were weak.

“Candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” one White House official told Fox News’s Peter Doocey on Tuesday night, amid the continued fallout. The official closed with a defiant note: “President Trump’s resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger,” they said. “Buckle up.”

Trump himself weighed in a few minutes later.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump posted on TruthSocial at 10:37 p.m. ET, shortly before multiple news networks called the Texas Senate race for Democrat James Talarico.

But Trump was, in some ways, on the ballot. It was his impact on the economy that Republican candidates were fighting against, his agenda that they were trying to defend, his rhetoric that they were trying to mimic. All of those factors had won the GOP elections before, in different economic conditions. But this year, voters saw only the worst. It also appears that while Trump might not admit fault, he does realize he’s been beaten. In an interview with the New York Times on Tuesday night, he said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results.”

Trump finished his Truth Social post with a familiar refrain: “Thank you for your attention to this matter.” His party is surely paying attention. With their losses in the midterms looking even worse than expected, the party will be searching for a way to reinvent itself with only two years left in its unpopular figurehead’s last term. #3372. Apple says memory costs and Siri AI will weigh on holiday quarter profit margins

Following today’s earnings report, Apple held its quarterly earnings call, during which the company discussed the impact of rising memory costs on its profit margins and warned of additional pressure from Siri AI expenses during the holiday quarter. Here are the details.

Over the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

Today, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.

Against the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:

“We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”

Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.

He attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.

When asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.

This, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:

“Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”

Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.

Ternus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.

#3371. Kansas Elects Its First Democratic Senator in 94 Years

Methodist minister Adam Hamiliton, a Democrat, has defeated Republican Roger Marshall in the race to represent Kansas in the U.S. Senate, ending a Democratic dry spell that has lasted nearly a century.

The mild-mannered megachurch pastor, who has been registered as a Republican, a Democrat, and an Independent over the course of his lifetime, assembled a broad coalition of voters in the heartland state, en route to pulling off one of the most improbable wins of the year in a state Donald Trump carried by over 16 percent just two years ago.

Marshall sought to paint his rival, the founding pastor of the largest united Methodist church in the country,  as “too woke” and “too weak” to represent Kansas, but voters appeared receptive to Hamiliton’s brand of scripture-laced centrism. “I’m pretty sure if Jesus were here [Marshall would] consider him too woke,” Hamilton said during his campaign.

In 2020, Marshall was re-elected with a margin of more than 11 points. This year, a surprisingly strong challenge from Hamilton, a difficult environment for Republicans, and new reporting about Marshall’s aggressive efforts to recoup payment from patients he treated when he was a practicing OB-GYN proved too much for the GOP nominee to overcome.

In polls throughout the election cycle, voters in Kansas consistently and overwhelmingly pointed to the economy as their top concern. In a state where nearly 90 percent of land is used for farming and ranching, the Republican candidate was damaged by the rising price of diesel gas — a side effect of the U.S. ongoing war with Iran — as well as the president’s decision to allow beef to be imported into the country at lower tariff rates.

Marshall, who was an OB-GYN before running for Senate, was hurt by the revelations that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of patients who failed to pay their medical bills. The New York Times reported in September that at least 81 of Marshall’s patients were arrested for missing court dates related to their debts, including a pregnant woman with a 2-year-old daughter. That woman, Meischa Zimmerman, had been uninsured when Marshall delivered her child via a c-section in 2009; she was arrested three times as Marshall pursued payment. Marshall told the Wall Street Journal that his only regret was not issuing a response earlier: “I would have been glad to put it out much, much sooner.”  Trending Stories Trump Is Already Crying That He’s Not to Blame for Republican Wipeout Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and 'You Can See Everything' Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

In the end, neither the ad nor two visits a piece from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance were enough to salvage Marshall’s reelection bid. During his latest visit to the state just days before the election, Trump called Hamilton a “perverted pastor,” but the newly elected senator took the insult in stride, pledging to work with the president regardless of the invective thrown his way.

“Anything the president wants to do that’s good for the people of Kansas, I will be his best partner here,” Hamilton said.

#3369. Apple forecasts its biggest revenue quarter ever despite supply constraints

During today’s earnings call following its fiscal Q4 2026 report, Apple said it expects its December quarter “to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.” Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with revenue climbing 12% year over year to $114.5 billion and net profit reaching $30.71 billion. This marked September-quarter records on both fronts, despite supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and iPad, as well as rising memory costs.

During the conference call following the earnings report, Apple acknowledged that higher memory costs were putting pressure on its profit margins, while also warning of limited supply-chain flexibility, stronger-than-expected demand for Mac and iPad, and ongoing shortages of the new iPhone Duo.

Still, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh was very clear about what the company expects from the next fiscal quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season:

We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between 7 and 10% year over year, which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.

If this pans out, Apple’s fiscal Q1 2027 revenue should fall between $153.82 billion and $158.13 billion, adding between $10 billion and $14.4 billion in revenue compared to the year-ago quarter.

Beyond revenue, Parekh also shared Apple’s expectations for several other financial metrics during the December quarter:

Parekh noted that “third-party licensing and foreign exchange” will be the primary headwinds for the Services revenue, while higher memory costs and “some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI” are expected to put further pressure on the company’s gross margins.

Finally, Apple cautioned that its outlook “assumes that global tariff rates, policies, and their application remain in effect as of this call, and the global macroeconomic outlook does not worsen from today.“

Apple shares fell as much as 4.43% in after-hours trading on Monday during the company’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, before recovering some of those losses later in the evening. Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with a 12% increase in revenue, another 12% increase in net profit, and record revenue from its Services category, following its first sequential quarterly decline in 15 quarters.

The results also included a 17% increase in iPhone revenue and a 24% increase in Mac revenue, but an 8% decline in Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue, which Apple attributed to “a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year,” and a 10% decline in iPad revenue, which Apple attributed to supply constraints and a similarly difficult comparison against last year’s A16-powered iPad launch.

Hopefully Apple can use this aberration in trading algorithms to cancel as many shares as possible on the cheap!

#3367. Democrats Win Total Control of Congress

The Democratic Party won total control of Congress in the midterm elections, part of a seismic, nationwide rebuke of Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

The party was widely expected to win back control of the House of Representatives, but less certain was the balance of the Senate. Democrats won them both, though, as part of a hugely successful night capping off one of the most chaotic, contested, and bitter midterm elections in recent history.

Riding a wave of voter turnout amid an economic crisis started by Republican President Donald Trump, Democratic Senate candidates won big in battleground states like Michigan, Georgia, and Maine, as well as in traditionally red states like Texas, Kansa, and South Carolina.

With a majority in the Senate and House, Democrats are now free to pursue an ambitious legislative agenda during Trump’s last two years in office. Trump is entering his lame duck period as a deeply unpopular president beset by scandal and crises of his own making. While he will likely use his presidential veto to keep many of a Democratic Congress’ bills from passing, control over both Houses will give the Democrats a powerful platform to both investigate Trump’s actions in the first half of his second term and set the tone for their agenda going into the next open presidential election in 2028.

“They will turn every committee of Congress into an investigative body, and they’ll go after the president’s family, the Cabinet, his donors and friends,” Speaker of the House Mike Johnson told a room of Christian conservatives earlier this year. “Half of you in this room will be targeted. I run the protection program. I’ll take care of you,” he added.

#3366. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3364. Keisha Lance Bottoms Makes History as First Black Woman Elected Governor

Keisha Lance Bottoms has won the Georgia governor’s race, becoming the first Black female governor elected in the United States. Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire businessman Rick Jackson, marking the first time the swing state has elected a Democratic governor in more than two decades.

The victory was a highlight in a massively successful night for Democrats in one of the most bitter midterm elections in recent history, one that saw the Democratic Party win total control of Congress in a nationwide rebuke of Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

Democratic Senate candidates won big in battleground states including Georgia, where Jon Ossoff was re-elected; Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton; and South Carolina, where pediatrician Annie Andrews claimed the South Carolina Senate seat. In another historic first, Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate race, and will be the first openly gay male senator with his victory over Republican John Sununu.

Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor who also served as an adviser in the Biden administration, won despite a colossal spending disadvantage against Jackson, who pumped tens of millions of his own fortune into his campaign.

Bottoms, like other Democrats across the nation, wielded frustration over the Trump administration to bolster a campaign that remained tightly focused on taking on the rising cost of living and quality of life issues. During her bid for governor, Bottoms proposed allowing local municipalities to eliminate the sales tax on groceries along with taxes on diapers, baby formula and feminine hygiene products. She also proposed doing away with the state income tax for public school teachers and the state’s tax on car insurance premiums, homeowner’s insurance, and gas. Bottoms also vowed to expand Medicaid and to pause the construction of new data centers in Georgia. #3362. Apple recently notified users in 99 countries of potential mercenary spyware attacks

Apple reportedly sent notifications to users in 99 countries warning of potential mercenary spyware attacks, as German authorities investigate reports that lawmakers and government officials may have been targeted. Here are the details.

A couple of reports from The Financial Times and TechCrunch today offer complementary details about a new wave of Apple threat notifications warning users that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.

As we’ve covered before, Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to users it believes may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks. The company doesn’t disclose who may be behind the attacks or confirm whether a device has been compromised, but advises recipients to take the warnings seriously and seek expert assistance.

You can learn more about Apple’s recommendations for protecting against mercenary spyware, including how to enable Lockdown Mode, here.

Back to today’s reports, The Financial Times says that German lawmakers and government officials began receiving threat notifications from Apple last Thursday, prompting the country’s Federal Office for Information Security to issue an urgent warning over the weekend.

The agency advised recipients to “assume their device is no longer secure,” while the German government said it was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously” and “working flat out to investigate the circumstances of the incident.”

The FT noted that German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius declined to say whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those affected, and added that the attacks reportedly exploited a “zero-click” vulnerability, allowing attackers to compromise devices without any interaction.

Knowledge of their targets’ phone numbers was all that the hackers needed to carry out the attack.

As it reported on the alerts, TechCrunch noted that “others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple,” including Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, who shared his alert on X.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

Mortada also noted in his tweet that he had previously been targeted by Pegasus spyware in 2017 and 2021, and that he does not know who was behind the latest attempt or whether it was connected to an investigative documentary he directed.

#3361. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

For the past few weeks, there have been so many instances of AI being used to tinker around with popular video games.

That practice has led to the trend of video game decompilations, which is the process of a developer working backward from a compiled, machine-code game to reconstruct readable, human-understandable source code. Reverse engineering games has also popped up as of late, which is all about a developer analyzing compiled machine code or raw binary files to understand their internal logic, rebuild that source code or port games to new platforms.

Because of those AI uses in connection with video games, Halo: Combat Evolved has been made completely playable within a web browser, Super Mario 64 has been decompiled to also work as a playable title on PC and even game mashups have popped up in the form of Minecraft becoming playable in Elden Ring.

But when it comes to using AI tools to completely recreate those popular types of games, Anthropic is making sure that practice won’t be doable with its Claude Code and Opus 5.5 AI models. Here’s how the AI company is blocking any future attempts at prompting the recreation, reverse-engineering and cloning of identifiable video games.

News of Anthropic’s Claude update blocking the cloning of recognizable video games surfaced after a user on X named @chasmmmmmmmmmmm noticed a new rule added to Claude Code that’s meant to block prompts that request the recreation of existing titles. That rule, which is entitled “tengu_heron_brook,” puts forth the following edict:

“Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”

In response to that X user’s Tweet, Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic, gave this statement on the matter:

Witnessing Skate 3 skateboarding physics crossing over with Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 multiplayer maps and seeing Escape from Tarkov's gunplay, loot systems and extraction mechanics make their way into the fantasy realm of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim has come courtesy of AI coding assistants like Claude Opus 5.5.

What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

Abdul El-Sayed has defeated MAGA Republican Mike Rogers in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat. The win caps a remarkable run for the insurgent progressive — who ran on bringing prices down, making healthcare available for all, and AI regulation — and marks a significant blow to Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator in American history.

The race to replace outgoing Sen. Gary Peters — Democrat — became one of the most vitriolic of the cycle. El-Sayed, a Michigan native and epidemiological physician, was subjected to a barrage of attacks against his Muslim faith and Arab heritage.

Trump and Republicans accused El Sayed of having ties to terrorist groups — including claims that he and his mother were associated with the Muslim Brotherhood. Republicans — and some Democrats — also attempted to frame El-Sayed’s campaign activities alongside leftist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as a signal of his supposed extremist ideology. At campaign events, Trump continuously mocked El-Sayed’s heritage and name at rallies. Just a week before Election Day, Trump referred to El-Sayed as a “Jihadist Member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” who wanted to institute “Sharia Law” in the United States. Rogers seized on similar lines of attack after winning his own primary, even as he attempted to distance himself from Trump by calling for an end to his trade war with Canada.

Democrats countered with the big guns. Former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside El-Sayed in his tour of contested states, which included Michigan, Ohio, and Georgia. Obama mocked Trump’s obsession with asses and jaw lines and the male physique, and his fixation on remodeling and redecorating the White House.

“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said of the Senate candidate, drawing comparisons to the right’s attempts to question his own heritage and faith during his presidency.

One Democrat who didn’t get behind El-Sayed was his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. Throughout the primary, Stevens accused El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of [his] problems on Jewish Americans” in response to their policy difference over the war in Gaza. The divisions of the primary lingered through the general, and though she for months insisted she supported the Democratic ticket, she formally endorsed Rogers in a shocking move two days before the election. #3354. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.
