Tackling baked-on oven grease is rarely anyone’s favorite chore, but the shortcuts you take to get the job done could be silently wrecking your cooker.

According to one appliance expert, several well-meaning cleaning methods can damage your appliance’s surface and reduce its performance.

While you might feel confident with how to clean your oven, Ecem Uslubaş, senior product manager for cooking at Hotpoint, says, “a lot of common habits are based on what’s always been done rather than what works for each surface.”

And she adds, “Getting it wrong doesn’t always cause obvious damage straight away, but it can impact the performance of your appliance without regular care.”

So, before you slip on your household gloves and give your oven a deep clean, consider these six common oven-cleaning mistakes — and the safer routines you should adopt instead.

Reaching for the same abrasive scourer for the cooktop, the oven interior and the exterior trim is one of the most common habits.

“Enamel, glass and stainless steel all respond differently to abrasive materials," explains Uslubaş. “A sponge tough enough for baked-on food can leave fine scratches on glass or dull the finish on stainless steel over time.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Instead of using the same cleaning sponge for all surfaces, she suggests keeping a softer cloth aside for delicate surfaces and reserving anything abrasive for tougher, more durable areas, as it will help protect each surface for longer.

Wiping a spill away once the cooker has cooled is far easier than dealing with it after several more cooking cycles.

“Each time a spill gets reheated, it bonds more firmly to the surface,” says Uslubaş. “What would have taken a quick wipe on day one can end up needing a specialist product and more effort a few weeks later.”

Even though it can seem easy to close the oven door and pretend the mess doesn’t exist, it will only prolong and worsen the cleanup. Instead of a simple wipe-down, your oven will need a deep clean if spills are left to solidify and become baked-in.

Aiming a spray bottle straight at the controls can allow liquid to seep behind buttons or dials, which may affect how they function. However, there’s a simple way to change this habit, protecting your appliance while still getting it clean.

“It’s worth applying the product to a cloth first, rather than spraying it directly onto the panel,” advises Uslubaş.

Shelves, trays and other removable parts vary between cooker models, and not all of them are suited to a dishwasher cycle.

It's also worth being aware that some finishes can be affected by the heat or the detergents used in a dishwasher, which makes them unsuitable, while some parts may only be suitable for cleaning on the top rack.

Uslubaş says, "Make sure you check the appliance instructions before removing or washing any parts of your appliance. It’s also worth checking before using any specialist cleaning product too.”

Lining the bottom of the oven with foil might seem like a simple way to catch spills, but it can interfere with airflow and heat distribution. Although it's easier to remove and replace soiled foil, it has a negative impact on the performance of your oven.

"Ovens are designed with specific airflow in mind, and foil can disrupt that, leading to uneven cooking results," explains Uslubaş.

As an alternative she suggests using removable trays or liners designed for the purpose, as they are a safer way to catch drips without affecting performance.

This Whirlpool electric range features two ovens and has a combined capacity of 6.7 cubic feet, with plenty of space to cook multiple foods at different temperatures. Plus, with 5 burners and Aqua-Lift self-cleaning technology, it's hard to beat.

The door seal is one of the most frequently missed areas during a routine clean, despite playing an important role in how efficiently the oven heats. I have to admit, that I also neglect cleaning my washing machine and dishwasher seal, just the same.

"Seals can gather grease and food debris just like any other part of the oven, and a damaged or dirty seal can let heat escape," says Uslubaş. “Wiping around the seal and door edges as part of a regular clean helps maintain both hygiene and cooking performance.”

Regularly cleaning the seal also lets you check for wear, such as cracks that can reduce the seal’s efficiency.

Cleaning an oven can be a real drag, especially after you've cooked a roast, as the entire appliance can be covered in grease. But, it can be made easier by cleaning it out once it's cooled down, rather than leaving until it's cooked a few more dinners. However, if you are in the market for one of the best ovens, Uslubaş says it’s worth looking for an appliance that helps clean itself, and suggests buying one with the following features:Pyrolytic cleaningThe oven heats up to an extreme temperature and carbonizes and incinerates grease, baked-on food and residue to a fine ash.

Steam cleaningRather than heating to extreme temperatures, a steam cleaning function involves pouring a small amount of water onto the oven floor and heating it to around 200-400°F. The steam created helps loosen any residue, which can then be wiped away with a cloth.

Catalytic linersThe oven’s interior walls are lined with a porous enamel embedded with an oxidation catalyst. The liner continuously absorbs grease and food splatters while you’re baking at normal temperatures.

#3276. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.

#3274. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

Here’s how to tweak your device to help you reach your goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If one of your health goals is to lose weight, wearing a fitness tracker, including one of the best Apple Watches, is a great place to start. To lose weight and keep it off, you’ll need to ensure you’re burning more calories than you consume — otherwise known as a calorie deficit.

One of the easiest ways to see how many calories you’re burning is to wear a fitness tracker. Yet, if you’ve got an Apple Watch on your wrist, how you set up your watch can make all the difference. Read on to find out more.

As a reminder, if you’re looking for personalized advice when it comes to weight loss, it’s always a good idea to talk to your physician.

Whether you choose the Apple Watch SE 3, the Apple Watch Series 12, or invest in the Apple Watch Ultra 4, there are a few ways to ensure your watch gives you the most accurate health data. Here are three top tips:

Let’s caveat something here: no smartwatch or sports watch on the market will be 100% accurate when it comes to estimating how many calories you’ve actually burned. They largely rely on algorithms, and to really get an idea of your true energy expenditure every day, you’d need to be wired up in a lab.

That said, your Apple Watch will estimate your calorie expenditure using your heart rate data, as well as your personal metrics, plus data from the movement sensors and GPS. How accurately your watch records all of this data depends on how well it fits.

Your Apple Watch should be snug, not tight, with the heart rate sensor sitting flush against your wrist. The watch should sit above your wrist bone, and it shouldn’t be loose enough to rotate as you move.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Remember those personal metrics I just mentioned that form part of the calorie expenditure algorithm on your Apple Watch? It’s important to make sure these are accurate, especially as you start losing weight, because they can make a big difference.

It’s also important to ensure that your Apple Watch is calibrated, as this makes the data more accurate. Firstly, head to Location Services on your iPhone, click System Services, then Motion Calibration and Distance and make sure it’s turned on. Next, go for a 20-minute walk in a flat area where you can see clear blue skies (heavily wooded areas or skyscrapers can affect GPS) at your natural pace wearing the Apple Watch, as this will make sure it’s calibrated to your stride.

Finally, another important step when it comes to getting the most accurate idea of your calorie expenditure is to choose the right workout mode on your Apple Watch. Each workout type will use a specialized algorithm tailored to the expected movement pattern.

For example, I’d often use Functional Strength Training mode during my HIIT workouts in the gym. When I switched to using High-Intensity Interval Training, my average calorie burn was higher. This is because the Apple Watch is weighing the elevated heart rate that comes with a HIIT session with short periods of rest more heavily than it would in strength training mode.

Of course, even when your watch is set up perfectly, it’s important to reiterate again that no wearable will be perfect when it comes to estimating your overall calorie expenditure. The best way to lose weight is to eat a balanced, healthy diet, prioritize movement, and focus on your overall health.

#3270. Bitcoin briefly hits multi-week low as Democrats win Congress

Bitcoin briefly fell to its lowest level in six weeks on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both the US Senate and House of Representatives in the midterm elections.

The result could complicate the crypto industry’s push for faster deregulation, Reuters reported.

The market recovered some of its losses shortly afterwards. Bitcoin was trading roughly flat at $78,070 by 07:15 GMT, while ether gained around 1% to $2,292, according to Reuters.

The political result comes at a difficult time for the crypto market, which was already under pressure following last week’s $6.3bn Binance hack, the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

By Tuesday, customers had withdrawn a net $4.72bn from the exchange since it reopened following the attack.

The crypto industry has spent more than $300m supporting candidates from both parties across the current and previous election cycles, Reuters reported.

The investment was intended to help secure legislation that would give US crypto companies greater legal certainty and establish clearer rules for operating in the country. A Democratic majority in both chambers could make that agenda harder to advance.

The latest decline adds to a prolonged downturn. Bitcoin has lost around 41% of its value since reaching a record above $122,000 in October 2025.

The total cryptocurrency market is now worth approximately $2.61tn, based on CoinMarketCap data cited by Reuters.

Around $300bn has disappeared from the market’s value in the past month alone. Concerns about whether heavy investment in AI will generate sufficient returns, combined with higher borrowing costs, have encouraged investors to move towards safer assets, including government bonds.

“The market may be re-evaluating the risk-reward profile of crypto assets,” Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey, told Reuters.

Sun said the recent series of hacks was also prompting investors to reconsider the risks of holding assets on cryptocurrency exchanges. At the same time, the shift in political power in Washington could delay new legislation for the sector.

The regulatory environment has changed considerably since Donald Trump returned to the White House.

His administration has pursued lighter enforcement, established a strategic bitcoin reserve, eased crypto companies’ access to banking services, and supported the passage of a federal stablecoin law.

Trump and members of his family also have business interests in the sector, including a meme coin and the World Liberty Financial platform. Political spending has extended beyond the crypto industry, too.

Elon Musk’s contributions to candidates and political groups during the midterm cycle reached a record $474m, according to The New York Times.

Whether you’re after a gripping horror flick, a compelling crime film, or something a little more romantic, there’s plenty to choose from. So, if any of these have been sitting on your watchlist, now might be the time to watch before they’re gone.

What it's about: In this horror movie, a masked serial killer known as the Heart Eyes Killer has spent years targeting couples on Valentine's Day. When advertising colleagues Ally (Olivia Holt) and Jay (Mason Gooding) are mistaken for a loved-up pair, they find themselves in the killer's crosshairs. Forced to spend the most romantic night of the year fighting for their lives, the unlikely duo must put their differences aside to survive.

Why you should watch it: “Heart Eyes” is a bloody good time if you enjoy your horror with a healthy dose of comedy. I also love how it plays around with familiar slasher tropes, including gruesome kills and creepy moments with plenty of laughs. It's a fun, entertaining watch that doesn't take itself too seriously.

Watch "Heart Eyes" on Netflix until Nov. 8

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What it's about: After a series of brutal murders in a small New Mexico town, two FBI agents arrive to investigate and question three survivors: a troubled police officer, a drug-addicted young woman and an eight-year-old girl. However, the conflicting accounts reveal that not everyone is telling the truth, and the real story is far more disturbing than it first appears.

However, Kenna finds an unexpected ally in Ledger (Tyriq Withers), a local bar owner with connections to her daughter's family.

Maika Monroe delivers a strong lead performance, bringing plenty of feeling to a story about grief, forgiveness and getting a second chance at happiness. The movie has all the ingredients fans have come to expect from Hoover's work, including complicated relationships and some genuinely moving moments. Keep the tissues handy for this one!

#3267. Emirates SkyCargo launches AI Tech to fly server racks, chips and GPUs

Emirates SkyCargo will fly 23 dedicated freighters by March 2027, with main decks that fit server racks weighing more than 3.5 tonnes. Shipments are tracked from its command centre in Dubai.

An Emirates SkyCargo Boeing 777F freighter at Dubai Airport.

Emirates SkyCargo has a new product for companies building out artificial intelligence. AI Tech is designed to move critical and sensitive AI infrastructure safely and on time, the cargo arm of Emirates said in a press release.

It is built for capital equipment and other critical hardware as well as server racks. The service adds priority loading and scheduling, specialised handling and shipment monitoring from the airline’s command centre in Dubai. Emirates SkyCargo says the aim is to keep customers’ deployment schedules on track.

“Behind every AI breakthrough is physical infrastructure that needs to arrive safely and on time,” said Badr Abbas, divisional senior vice president at Emirates SkyCargo.

“In July alone, we transported more than 700 tonnes of AI infrastructure across our global network, and demand has continued to grow,” Abbas said.

He said the airline wants to become “the carrier of choice” for companies across the AI ecosystem.

AI Tech uses the same handling procedures at every airport. They keep equipment the right way up and cut the risk of damage. Time-critical deployments get priority loading.

Customers get airport-to-airport tracking, with milestone updates watched from the Dubai command centre. Staff keep in touch with customers throughout the journey. Oversized and heavy loads get specialist project cargo support.

The service is open across the airline’s network for most AI cargo, including chips and server racks. For highly specialised manufacturing equipment, Emirates SkyCargo checks each station’s capabilities before the shipment.

By March 2027, Emirates SkyCargo will fly 23 dedicated freighters. Their main decks can take tall, dense server racks, which often weigh more than 3.5 tonnes. The airline’s website lists 12 dedicated freighters today, alongside more than 260 wide-body aircraft.

The airline also carries cargo on its wide-body passenger aircraft. It flies to more than 270 destinations in 83 countries and territories.

Server racks are the hardware that makers such as Supermicro build around Nvidia GPUs and other AI chips. Big Tech has committed more than $3 trillion to the AI build-out. In Emirates’ home country, the UAE is splitting up its $30bn AI data centre after Iran named it as a target.

#3266. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3265. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

How to guarantee a spectacular Christmas cactus display

If you’re staring at your Christmas cactus right now and seeing nothing but plain green leaves, don't panic. There is still time to turn things around. The plant is notoriously finicky about its fall cues, and even a sliver of hallway light or a radiator turned up too high can stall budding entirely.

Fortunately, triggering a full flush of winter blooms doesn't require specialist gear or green fingers. A few precise changes to where it sits, how much you water it, and when you plunge it into darkness will kickstart the budding process in days.

If your cactus has stalled, light pollution is almost always the culprit. Christmas cacti rely on long, uninterrupted nights to trigger their bloom cycle, meaning even a stray hallway light or the glow from a television can fool the plant into thinking it is still summer.

To kickstart flowering, give it 12 to 14 hours of continuous darkness every evening, either by moving it into a spare bedroom or placing a light-blocking cardboard box over the pot.

Pair that blackout routine with a drop in temperature, aiming for around 55°F to 60°F (13°C to 16°C) overnight, before returning it to bright, indirect sunlight during the day.

When central heating kick on in November, it's tempting to panic and pour on extra water. Resist the urge. Soggy soil will rot the cactus’s delicate root system within days, while bone-dry compost will cause any newly forming flower buds to shrivel and abort before they ever open.

Keep things simple: poke a finger into the top inch of soil and only water when it feels dry, making sure to empty out any runoff sitting in the saucer beneath. Your target is light, consistent moisture.

Now is the moment to stop trying to feed your way out of the problem. If you have been giving your plant liquid houseplant fertilizer over summer, cut it off entirely. Pumping nutrients into the soil now will confuse the plant, forcing out limp leafy pads at the expense of flower buds.

You should also hold off on repotting, no matter how tight the pot looks. Christmas cacti actually bloom best when they are slightly root-bound, and disturbing the root ball in late fall shocks the plant into survival mode. Tuck the fertilizer away and leave the roots completely undisturbed until spring.

Once tiny pink, red, or white nodules finally start appearing at the tips of the green segments, the biggest danger is bud drop.

Christmas cacti are easily stressed once buds appear. Rotating the pot, shifting it to a new windowsill, or exposing it to an open-door draft can cause it to jettison weeks of progress right onto the floor.

Pick a single, consistent spot with good indirect light, keep it well away from direct radiator heat or open windows, and do not touch it again until those buds are fully open and ready to show off.

#3262. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

#3260. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

If you haven't already heard about polarized training, let me give you a very quick summary: the 80/20 rule refers to an endurance training technique that works between two workout intensities — 80% low intensity and 20% high intensity while removing the middle "grey zone."

It's based on a model popularized by Dr. Stephen Seiler, and elite athletes from rowers to runners have been using it to dial into their training loads. By properly utilizing low training load, your body can recover enough to maximize high training load, leading to better endurance over time without overtraining.

But not everyone has one of the best fitness trackers to look at the data, so I paced the 80/20 rule without the workout tech. No smartwatches or apps in sight. Here's how.

According to Seiler, the zones are split as follows:

As briefly mentioned, low effort doesn't mean low reward; easier paces are essential for recovery and building a strong aerobic base. It might feel frustrating, but that doesn't mean it's a bad thing.

Let's look at one piece of research published in the International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance as an example. The study assessed 30 endurance runners assigned either low-intensity, sub-ventilatory-threshold, polarized endurance training or a moderately high-intensity program. The researchers concluded that polarized training methods could stimulate greater training effects than "between-threshold" training in runners.

In other words, using high- and low-intensity efforts combined can provide the most gains: high output for pace and power, and low intensity for increased cardiovascular strength and better recovery.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Most importantly, zone 1 training should sit below the lactate threshold, meaning your effort is below an intensity where lactate accumulates, which is when exercise goes from aerobic (with oxygen) to anaerobic (without oxygen). Your high-effort runs should feel very challenging. Try to avoid or minimize these middle-ground efforts that feel challenging yet manageable.

My main takeaway from this is that I'd have to get comfortable with moving slower and faster than I'd like. My comfort zone as a recreational runner is firmly in the middle, unless I'm working on sprint intervals on a treadmill.

Unused to this style of training, it would have been easier to set up heart rate zones on my sports watch so that I could accurately track my efforts and the percentages of my maximum heart rate. For example, I recently set up zone 2 cardio on my Coros Pace 4, and could tailor all my workouts to my heart rate.

But I like a challenge, so instead I used something personal trainers have used for years in the fitness industry: rate of perceived exertion, or RPE.

For easy runs, I stayed at around 4/10 effort, what I perceive as my conversational pace. This is an effort I can sustain for hours if needed, so I could quickly identify what speed to stay at. I programmed this for 80% of my efforts. For the other 20% I worked at 8-9/10, which is a pace I could only sustain for short bursts, or for a slightly longer duration, around 7/10, still close to my max.

The goal? Improve VO2 max (my heart's capacity to pump oxygenated blood around my body) while also improving power output, speed and anaerobic abilities without burning out or injuring myself. After all, if you're constantly working somewhere in the middle, you're never really achieving those sought-after training adaptations, and you're also never fully recovered for a hard effort.

To think about this using percentages, those hard efforts should be roughly 90% of your maximum heart rate. Here's an example of a hard effort:

Remember, too much high-intensity training can have a negative impact on hormones and can keep your body in the sympathetic nervous system for longer than it needs to be. Over time, this can lead to burnout, muscle fatigue, injuries and stress. You need to incorporate active recovery and easy days regardless of what training you enjoy, as this is where the real growth happens.

For me, one hard running session in the gym is enough, with a few easy runs peppered in. This meant turning up seriously ready for a hard push on the days I knew I was well rested.

#3258. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

#3257. India’s EloElo raises $80M from NBCUniversal and Hornbill for Story TV

EloElo’s four apps reach more than 40 million monthly users and 300 million installs. NBCUniversal says it will help the company expand beyond India, including into the US.

EloElo Group, the Bengaluru company behind the Indian microdrama app Story TV, has raised $80 million in a Series C round. Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal co-led it, the company said in a statement. MIT Investment Co. joined, with existing backers Play Ventures, Kalaari Capital, Waterbridge Ventures and Griffin Gaming Partners.

The round values EloElo at $500 million, Ivan Mehta reported for TechCrunch. It takes the company’s total funding to $130 million.

“Story TV shows us what India wants to watch, and Dolphin AI gives us the economics to make it,” said founder and chief executive Saurabh Pandey.

Pandey, a former Flipkart executive, founded EloElo in 2020. Story TV carries more than 5,000 microdramas in six languages and adds a new one every three hours. Users spend 95 minutes a day on the app, according to the company.

The group also runs Master, a micro learning app, and Voxy AI, an AI companion. Dolphin AI is its agentic AI creative suite, which makes images, audio and video. Across the four apps, EloElo counts more than 40 million monthly active users and 300 million installs.

EloElo says its revenue grew several times over in the past year. It started charging users in May 2024. It reported revenue of Rs 69.5 crore for the year to March 2025, Harsh Upadhyay reported for Entrackr. Its previous round was a $13.5 million Series B in April 2025.

EloElo will spend the money on original shows in local languages, a launch of its microdramas outside India and more work on Dolphin AI. The company has 240 staff and wants to grow its AI and machine learning research team, TechCrunch reported.

“We’re excited to bring NBCUniversal’s global capabilities to the partnership as EloElo expands beyond India, including into the U.S. market,” said Deepak Arya, executive vice president of corporate strategy and development at NBCUniversal.

In its statement, EloElo cited Omdia’s forecast that microdramas will generate $14 billion worldwide by the end of 2026. It also cited Redseer’s estimate that 40 million Indians paid for a microdrama at least once in the year to March 2026.

In China, the state has backed AI microdrama production, and people now license their faces for AI-made microdramas. NBCUniversal’s Peacock, meanwhile, will come with YouTube Premium from 2027.

These are the shows I wouldn’t overlook this week

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There’s always something worth watching on Prime Video, but with so many shows competing for a place on the trending list, figuring out what deserves a spot on your watchlist can be tricky. The streamer’s top 10 shows list is actually a handy place to start, but not everything trending is necessarily worth binge-watching. So, I’ve picked out three shows from this week’s rankings that I think are worth your time.

That includes a little something for everyone, whether you’re after a gritty action-thriller now streaming its second season, a crime comedy pairing an unlikely duo with plenty of chemistry, or a lighthearted romantic drama full of unexpected connections. They offer three very different viewing experiences, but each has something that makes it worth adding to your watchlist. Here’s what I’d be checking out this week.

This list is based on the Prime Video U.S. top 10 shows as of Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

Prime Video’s “The Terminal List” is back, and it’s clearly still a hit with viewers, currently sitting at No. 1 on the platform’s charts. Based on Jack Carr’s bestselling military thriller novels, the action-packed series also leans into its psychological drama and the emotional weight that comes with these experiences. After a four-year wait since its 2022 debut, all eight episodes of season 2 are now available to stream, giving fans plenty to get stuck into. If you enjoy shows like “Reacher” and “Tom Clancy’s Jack Ryan,” this should be your next pick.

James Reece (Chris Pratt) is a Navy SEAL commander whose entire platoon is ambushed during a covert mission. After returning home with conflicting memories of what happened, Reece begins investigating the operation and discovers that the people responsible may be closer to home than he ever imagined. As he follows a trail of evidence, he finds himself caught up in a far-reaching government conspiracy. Season 2 picks up after Reece completes his revenge mission, following him as he’s drawn into a new operation involving the CIA, a former ally and a resurgent Al-Qaeda network.

Fancy something a little lighter after all the action and drama? “Wild Cards” is a fun crime series that should be right up your alley if you enjoyed shows like “Psych,” “White Collar” or “Castle.” It has witty banter and an entertaining central partnership with plenty of episodic mysteries, making it an easy show to dip in and out of. All 10 episodes of season 3 are now available on Prime Video, so you can catch up at your own pace without needing to buy individual episodes or sign up for an extra subscription. It’s a great choice when you want something entertaining.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Wild Cards” follows the unlikely partnership between demoted detective Cole Ellis (Giacomo Gianniotti) and clever con artist Max Mitchell (Vanessa Morgan). After Max is arrested and helps Ellis solve a local case, the pair are offered a chance to turn things around. The catch is that they have to work together, with Ellis relying on traditional police work and Max using her talent for disguises, elaborate schemes and talking her way into almost any situation. As they investigate a new case each week, the two gradually learn how to work as a team, despite their very different approaches to solving crimes.

“Love in Disguise” is a fun South Korean series that puts a fresh spin on the romantic comedy formula by adding a little mystery and suspense. Based on the popular Kakao web novel, the show brings together the playful chaos of a gender-swap rom-com with the twists of a corporate thriller. It’s a slightly different take on the K-drama formula, giving viewers plenty of romantic complications alongside a more suspenseful storyline. If you enjoy Korean dramas that offer romance, comedy and a few unexpected twists, this one is worth checking out.

Kang Jae-hee (Seol In-ah) is a former special forces officer turned detective who goes undercover to investigate Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), the wealthy heir to a powerful business empire and the prime suspect in his secretary’s murder. To get close to him and uncover evidence, Jae-hee disguises herself as a man and takes a job as his personal secretary. However, keeping her real identity under wraps isn’t easy, especially as Yi-jun becomes increasingly suspicious of his new employee. As the investigation progresses, their complicated working relationship takes some unexpected turns.
