#3213. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

#3212. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3211. Warren Buffett's 3 Longest-Held Stocks Average a 3,757% Gain and Collectively Deliver $1.53 Billion in Annual Dividend Income for Berkshire Hathaway

The Oracle of Omaha’s patience has paid off handsomely for his company and its shareholders.

For the first time in well over half a century, Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.22%)(BRKB +0.17%) entered the year in uncharted territory. The company's longtime CEO, Warren Buffett, hung up his work coat for the final time at the end of last year, passing the baton to his protégé, Greg Abel.

Though Abel completely overhauled the company's $362 billion investment portfolio in the first quarter, the Oracle of Omaha left his understudy on solid footing. The three longest-held stocks in Berkshire's portfolio -- Coca-Cola (KO -1.07%), American Express (AXP -0.76%), and Moody's (MCO -0.46%) -- have delivered an average return of 3,757% (as of Oct. 30, 2026), and are collectively producing almost $1.53 billion in annual dividend income.

Warren Buffett's longest-tenured holdings are crushing it! Image source: Getty Images.

Beverage giant Coca-Cola is Berkshire Hathaway's most-tenured holding. It's been held continuously since 1988, leading to a nearly 2,800% return, not including dividends.

But dividends are the real star here. Coca-Cola has raised its base annual payout for 64 consecutive years. The $2.12 per share it pays out yearly, compared to Berkshire's $3.2475 cost basis in Coca-Cola, works out to an annual yield on cost of better than 65%! Buffett's company is nearly doubling its initial $1.3 billion investment in Coca-Cola from the dividends alone every 18 months.

Coca-Cola's recipe for success continues to be its geographic diversity and global brand appeal. It has operations in all but three countries (North Korea, Cuba, and Russia), enabling it to move the organic growth needle in emerging markets, while generating predictable cash flow in foundational developed countries.

Credit-services titan American Express, known best as Amex, has been continuously held by the Oracle of Omaha's company since 1991 and has rallied 3,659% from a cost basis of around $8.49 per share.

Although Amex hasn't raised its dividend as regularly as Coca-Cola, it's grown significantly over the last 35 years. Its $3.80-per-share payout translates into a mouthwatering annual yield on cost of roughly 45% for Berkshire Hathaway.

American Express's long-term outperformance reflects its ability to benefit from both sides of the transaction counter. In the U.S., it's firmly the No. 3 payment processor by credit-card network purchase volume and is also a core lender to businesses and consumers. This allows it to generate merchant fees from facilitating payments, as well as annual fees and interest income from its cardholders.

Though it's the smallest of the three positions, credit-ratings agency Moody's has delivered the most robust gains. Its shares have climbed by more than 4,800% since its spinoff from Dun & Bradstreet in September 2000.

Moody's has increased its base annual dividend for 16 consecutive years. The $4.12 per share it's currently doling out equates to a 41% yield on cost next to Berkshire's cost basis of around $10.05 per share.

Moody's parabolic ascent since the start of the century reflects strong demand for its credit-rating services amid a prolonged period of low interest rates. The company's Analytics segment, covering everything from risk assessment to regulatory compliance, has also gained traction over time.

#3208. Palantir Just Did This for the First Time Ever. Is the Stock a Buy?

Palantir just delivered another blowout earnings report.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR -1.65%) has been one of the early winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. The company sells AI-driven software that helps customers aggregate and make better use of their data. Customers have flocked to Palantir's software as it offers them an opportunity to easily apply AI to their needs -- without having to develop a platform on their own.

This has translated into tremendous growth for Palantir over the past couple of years, and this continued in the company's latest blowout earnings report. Third-quarter revenue soared in the double digits, and Palantir lifted several full-year forecasts.

On top of this, Palantir did one thing in particular for the first time ever -- and this is something that could determine what comes next. Is the stock a buy?

So, first, let's talk a bit about Palantir's business. The company has been around for more than 20 years, offering platforms that help customers leverage the power of their data. A few years ago, Palantir launched its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), integrating large language models into its system. The company holds bootcamps to introduce customers to AIP, and through these sessions, they can go from zero to a use case in a matter of hours.

This has proven to be successful, as earnings have taken off at Palantir, and investors have piled into the stock to benefit.

The recent quarter represented another wave of growth for Palantir, with the company delivering a 96% increase in revenue to $2.3 billion and a Rule of 40 score of 158%. This metric measures a software company's ability to balance growth with profitability, and a level of 40% is seen as good. So, at 158%, which represents the 13th straight quarterly gain, Palantir truly is winning.

The company, confident about the full year, raised its revenue forecast as well as forecasts for U.S. commercial revenue, adjusted income from operations, and adjusted free cash flow.

Now, let's consider the one thing in particular that Palantir did for the first time ever: Palantir's U.S. commercial revenue surpassed its U.S. government revenue. They came in at $984 million and $953 million, respectively. And while the former advanced in the triple digits, the latter rose in the double digits.

Though government revenue remains a core part of the Palantir story, this shows a clear shift into the commercial market. It's significant because for most of the company's history, it's relied on government contracts for growth. Today, it has greatly broadened its revenue stream, and this increasing number of clients means less risk. Palantir had fewer than 20 U.S. commercial customers a few years ago, and now, that number has grown to more than 600.

I see this as a significant driver of growth moving forward as companies look for ways to apply AI quickly and easily -- without having to start from scratch on their own.

Considering all of this, is Palantir a buy right now? It's important to consider your investing strategy and comfort with risk before deciding. Cautious investors may not like certain elements, such as Palantir's valuation. Though it's come down considerably from earlier levels, the stock is still expensive at more than 100x forward earnings estimates.

Some investors might also worry about slowing growth in new U.S. commercial contract value; the company closed $1.4 billion in the third quarter, representing 11% growth, while in the second quarter, this metric advanced 153% to $2.1 billion. That said, contract signings may not always translate into linear growth; growth could ebb and flow while still supporting solid earnings gains over time.

Palantir may not be the best investment for cautious investors. But considering the company’s track record of growth in recent years and the emergence of the commercial customer as a major growth driver, the stock makes a great buy for more aggressive investors who aim to hold on for the long run.

#3206. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

#3203. Will Crypto Rally After the Midterm Elections? If History Is Any Guide, This Happens Next.

Crypto has only been around since 2009, but the sector's movement following midterms shows a clear trend.

Although most investors try to avoid daily headlines and not focus too much on politics when evaluating stocks, they also know that politics can't be avoided altogether.

After all, policy and regulation can have a big effect on many stocks. That's why investors pay attention to the U.S. midterm elections. If there is a change in the controlling party in Congress, it could affect a sector's outlook.

Since President Donald Trump took office and the Republicans gained control of Congress in early 2025, cryptocurrencies have enjoyed a much more supportive regulatory environment.

But what will happen to crypto after the midterms? Will the sector rally after a tumultuous year? If history is any guide, this will happen next.

Equities have historically enjoyed a strong run after midterm elections, and so has crypto in its short existence.

Bitcoin (BTC +1.15%), the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, was essentially created right after the worst of the 2008 Great Recession, when many people lost faith in the mainstream financial system. It was originally viewed as an alternative currency, although it has since morphed into an investment.

This means it has been around for four midterm elections. The end of midterms has historically led to a rally in stocks because it removes uncertainty and provides the market with greater clarity on what policy and regulation could look like during the next two to four years.

Crypto is often more volatile than equities, so it's not a huge surprise to learn that Bitcoin, a bellwether for crypto, has performed exceptionally well in the year after midterm elections, according to data from TradingView and CoinDesk:

The crypto market was still in its early stages in 2010 and much smaller than it is today. Excluding that cycle, Bitcoin gained an average of 54% in the year after the past midterm elections, according to CoinDesk.

Investors should remember that although history rhymes, it rarely repeats, so this time could certainly be different.

As I mentioned, crypto has enjoyed a very friendly regulatory environment in the U.S. Trump has issued executive orders to create a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and to make it easier for retirement accounts to invest in crypto.

Additionally, Congress has passed legislation such as the Genius Act, creating a regulatory framework for stablecoins. However, Republicans have been unable to pass the Clarity Act, which would clear up many regulatory gray areas, such as which regulatory body has jurisdiction over certain cryptocurrencies.

Democrats aren't entirely opposed to passing crypto legislation. If they regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, which they are favored to do, they will likely, at the very least, require more concessions from Trump, such as adding more ethics provisions to the bill.

The other thing to remember is that crypto is still a fairly new industry, having only really been established in early 2009. Four midterms isn't a huge sample size, and it's really only three, given how small the crypto market was in 2010.

Additionally, investors should consider that Bitcoin tends to benefit from its halving event, which occurs every four years. During this event, miners see their rewards for validating Bitcoin transactions and minting new blocks cut in half.

That effectively slows supply growth, which is the main reason investors purchase Bitcoin in the first place: its finite supply makes it at least appear to be a form of digital gold, and therefore a potential hedge against inflation.

Coincidentally, after Bitcoin's last four halvings, Bitcoin surged for the next 12 to 18 months or so and then fell into a bear market. These bear markets have occurred in the years leading up to midterms, so it's possible that Bitcoin and crypto began rallying after the bear market, rather than due to midterms.

That doesn't mean Bitcoin and crypto won't surge after midterms. But investors should remember that crypto is extremely volatile, so predicting near-term outcomes is difficult.

How to steer clear of danger while using an AI assistant to shop

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We’ve gotten to the point where people are relying on AI assistants to help them navigate all the madness associated with holiday shopping.

According to Bain & Company, nearly a quarter of US online shoppers plan to kick off their holiday shopping on an AI platform like ChatGPT or Gemini (which is a stat that’s up from 17% last year).

With that increase in AI tools being used to aid online shoppers comes the threat of scammers, who look to exploit those shoppers with fake online stores (which are now popping up at a current rate of one every three minutes). And what’s worse is that those same stores have now started showing up in AI assistants’ product recommendations.

In a bid to learn more about how to shop more safely when using AI for online shopping, how a holiday gift list given to AI could build out an identity map of your family and more, I spoke to cybersecurity expert Serena Sullivan.

Here’s hoping her advice makes your AI-assisted holiday shopping experience less susceptible to any sorts of scams.

Consumers often unintentionally disclose personal information. Depending on the way the user crafts their prompts into the AI engine, some information could be inferred.

For example, if the user is searching for personal care items to purchase as a gift, they could unintentionally reveal the gender and age of the person they are purchasing the gift for. If they search for ballet shoes, they could reveal the age range of the recipient, the gender, their hobbies and interests. If you are looking for gifts that are very expensive versus inexpensive, some conclusions could be drawn about the user’s disposable income.

If the person was looking for an experience instead of a gift, maybe a family trip to a theme park, AI could likely deduce the size of the family, whether any family members need accessibility options, which state or country they live in, and a generalization of how much income the family has access to.

Individually, these details might seem harmless. However, when combined, they can create a surprisingly detailed picture of someone's personal life. This is how a data aggregation attack works. An attacker can pull information using Open Source Intelligence (OSINT), meaning information that is freely available on the internet, to compile a detailed profile of the individual. This information can then be used to perform detailed phishing or other social engineering attacks through email, voicemail, phone, or text.

Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for.

Treat AI assistants as you would any other online service. Only share the information you are willing to disclose, keeping in mind that other information could be combined to create a detailed picture of the user and those they are purchasing gifts for.

Just because AI makes a recommendation does not mean that AI found the correct website and does not indicate that the website has been vetted for safety or security. Additionally, AI could present the shopper with an outdated link.

When you click a link provided in AI results, the first thing to check is if it is a secure website. For example, if the shopper is warned that the digital certificate is out of date or illegitimate, do not continue using that website. Other warning signs, beyond security, are if the items appear too good to be true. For example, if you know an item normally costs about $100 and this website is selling it for $10, it could be a scam.

Shoppers can also identify potential signs of scams by checking the website address and determining if it matches what was expected. For example, the shopper wants to buy a nice piece of jewelry for their significant other; let’s say they wanted to go to ringsforspecialpeople.com (please note this is a fake website, just for the example). When the shopper enters the website, they notice the domain name is not related; maybe it automatically turns into jewelryforspecialpeople.com.

The website could be an exact duplicate of the website the shopper is accessing, but it is not. This should not be confused with related domains. For example, many companies will purchase all the related domains and have them redirected to their main website. The owner of the website could have purchased jewelryforspecialpeople.com and have it redirected to the main website.

Shoppers can also navigate to the suggested website without clicking the link in the AI response. Instead of clicking the link, the shopper could use a search engine to search for that website and click the website from the search results.

Prospective buyers can also review the payment options the website provides. One red flag is if the website requests payment in the form of money orders, wire transfers, gift cards, or cryptocurrency. Those forms of payment are not typical. Most companies would prefer a credit card or payments through other sites, like PayPal, Apple Pay, and others.

Shoppers should be aware of the company they are doing business with. They can research the seller by verifying it is a legitimate company, read user reviews, and identify if they have a customer service department. Most scammers will not have a customer service department. Review the policies on the website.

The warning signs mentioned above apply regardless of how someone arrives at a website. Whether a shopper clicks a link provided by an AI assistant or finds the website through a traditional search engine, the same precautions should be taken. However, as AI increasingly generates recommendations based on individual shopping queries, fraudulent websites and scams may become more difficult to recognize, particularly when the results appear relevant, personalized, and legitimate.

The advancement of AI has given scammers the ability to create highly convincing websites, customer reviews, product descriptions, and chatbots. As a result, it can be increasingly difficult for shoppers to distinguish legitimate businesses from fraudulent ones.

However, consumers can take steps to verify a business before making a purchase. Researching the company, reviewing its Better Business Bureau (BBB) rating and complaint history, and checking for any current or past consumer protection lawsuits or regulatory actions can help shoppers determine whether a business is trustworthy.

If a website appears to be professional-looking, it does not necessarily indicate that the website is trustworthy. If a shopper has even the slightest inkling that the website may be fraudulent, they should research using some of these suggestions or find a different website that does not contain any of the red flags mentioned.

Just because AI makes a recommendation does not mean that AI found the correct website and does not indicate that the website has been vetted for safety or security.

Children would often like to be gifted technology items. However, parents should use caution when deciding what type of technology is appropriate for their child. I would stress that parents teach their children how to spot behaviors or platforms that might be attempting to collect information, or worse.

Many popular technology gifts have the capability of collecting personal information. Parents are the first line of defense for minimizing some of the risks associated with those types of products. If the gift includes options for using a microphone, cameras, location tracking, or has AI integrated, parents should pay particular attention to those capabilities and become familiar with parental controls.

AI-driven toys, like robots or interactive dolls, could record the child’s voice, save conversations and questions the child may ask. Other interactions could also be saved on the device, or in the cloud if it is connected to the internet. If the toy connects to the internet, there is potential that an attacker could access that information.

Video games are a very common gift for children to receive. Games such as Roblox have a feature where children can talk and type to other users they are playing with. A safer approach is to use parental controls to block that feature from children.

If children are using personal assistants or planners and add significant dates, such as birthdays, vacations, school hours, extracurricular activities, and similar, that could be dangerous if an attacker compromises that data. The attacker would potentially be privy to household schedules, how many members are in the family, potentially gender, sexual orientation of family members, religious beliefs, or when the child would be away from home and where they are.

Smartwatches and fitness trackers can also pose potential danger. These devices may collect location information, activity patterns, contacts, and other personal information. Many of these devices are not covered under HIPAA, so they do not necessarily have the same protection applied as medical devices do.

Parents can ask themselves a few questions when evaluating the potential technology gift:

1. What information does the device collect?

2. Is audio, video, or location information stored in the cloud?

3. Who has access to that information, and is it shared with third parties?

4. Can parents disable microphones, cameras, and location tracking?

5. Does the manufacturer provide regular security updates?

6. Can parents review and permanently delete collected information?

Users should be careful about what they self-disclose.

Sharing general information about a family gathering, planning a holiday list, or finding the best gifts for their loved ones is a reasonable use of technology. However, one does not need to include things like full names, addresses, phone numbers, birth date, financial circumstances, sexual orientation, ethnicity, and other identifiable information. Users should consider sharing the bare minimum of information with the AI assistant that will allow it to perform as expected.

Certain information should never be provided to any AI-enabled device, such as:

Personally identifiable information, for adults and children, like Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport information, school schedules, extracurricular activities, or information that could allow an attacker to know where the user is physically located.

As a general rule of thumb, if you would not want anyone outside of your family and close friends to know the information, it should not be entered into the technology.

Anyone who is not familiar with technology or does not understand online safety practices can be especially vulnerable to scammers.

Older adults are often targeted because the scammers know their victims are unfamiliar with online safety and security measures and will use terminology to increase the likelihood that an inexperienced user might fall for the scam. Older adults make desirable victims because they may have more funds, like access to a retirement account, which could contain a large sum intended to last the retiree the rest of their life. Scammers will often try to create a sense of urgency, exploit trust, or play on emotions.

Scammers used to craft emails, websites, apps, and other methods of delivery, and they were often riddled with misspellings, logos that did not seem accurate, and incorrect grammar. With generative AI, scammers have reduced the likelihood of consumers immediately identifying the communication as a scam. By using AI and a few pointed prompts, scammers can now craft grammatically correct and spelling error-free communication. AI has made it much easier for everyone to develop websites and apps in a fraction of the time it used to take.

Creating more realistic content, combined with the ability to find publicly available information about their victim, has allowed scammers to develop realistic-looking communications that can be specifically targeted to their victim.

For example, Dr. Sullivan could have posted to an open Facebook account that she likes to take her corgi to the dog park. The attacker could create an email pretending to be from the city that owns the dog park, naming her dog, saying he was being banned because someone reported her dog as being aggressive. They could include an urgent deadline to have the situation rectified, increasing the chances that Dr. Sullivan would click on the link in the email.

When she clicks the link, it could take her to the fake dog park’s website that appears to be legitimate. Perhaps they will encourage her to pay a fine if she wants her dog to be allowed back in the park. Just that quickly, the attacker could now have a username and password she created on the website, along with her credit card information. That information could then be used to steal additional funds from her or start trying the username and password she provided to attempt to enter other accounts and websites.

Voice cloning is also easier to perform. All the attacker needs is a few-second clip of the voice, and they can generate illegitimate phone calls and other types of voice communications. Imagine a grandparent receiving a phone call in their grandchild’s voice, stating they are being held for ransom. The fake voice states that the grandparents must send a certain amount of cryptocurrency to see their grandchild again.

These situations have happened, and some have been tricked, while others knew it was not their grandchild, because the grandchild is sitting in the back seat of their car and could not be the same person on the telephone. If a familiar voice is saying unusual things, it is a great idea to double-check to determine if it was a legitimate phone call or not.

Families can protect themselves by using several precautions.

Tips on how to handle online scams are to slow down and think about the request, who is making the request, and how likely the request is to be legitimate. Scammers thrive on people making hasty decisions or acting out of emotions rather than thinking the situation through.

From the ransom situation described above to a fantastic and unbelievable deal on an item the person was researching as a gift, consumers should take a few minutes to ask for help from a tech-savvy family member or to think about the situation thoroughly before acting.

Here are a few suggestions on how to use AI in a safer manner.

So many AI platforms exist, so it would be impossible to list all of them here; only some of the most popular AI is listed here. If a person is using a different AI platform outside of what is listed here, users can perform a search to determine how to perform these actions on other platforms. Consumers should also be aware that even with these pointers and training, nothing is 100% secure.

Turning off model improvement does not automatically delete existing conversations, and temporary chats may also be retained for up to 30 days for safety purposes.

For specific details, conduct a search for ChatGPT Data Controls.

1. Protect your personal information: Do not share passwords, financial information, Social Security numbers, children's identifying information, or detailed travel schedules with AI assistants.

2. Verify every website and seller: Never assume an AI-recommended website is legitimate. Independently verify the retailer, domain name, seller reputation, and contact information before purchasing.

3. If a deal seems too good to be true, it probably isn’t true: Be cautious of unusually low prices, unexpected discounts, fast-approaching sales end, and requests for unusual payment methods. If something seems urgent, that is an indicator that consumers should slow down and independently verify the details.

5. Verify before you buy: Independently confirm the product, seller, total price, shipping costs, return policy, and payment method.

Details a consumer should verify before purchasing include ensuring the seller is legitimate, validating the details of the product being purchased, confirming the total cost, payment security, and available purchase protections.

Use credit cards for purchases whenever possible, as that allows consumers one more avenue to explore should they have followed all the safety tips and were scammed regardless.

#3199. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3198. 3 Nasdaq-100 Stocks That Can Double, According to Wall Street

Wall Street's median target prices suggest these are the three best Nasdaq-100 stocks to buy right now.

The Nasdaq-100 has created tremendous wealth for long-term investors. Over the last 10 years, the growth-focused index has returned 20.6% annually, easily outperforming the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.36%), which returned 15.5% annually.

The three Nasdaq-100 stocks listed below have the highest implied upside among index constituents, based on Wall Street's median target prices. In fact, consensus estimates suggest all three stocks could double investors' money over the next year.

Here's what investors should know about these growth stocks.

CoreWeave operates a cloud computing platform built specifically for artificial intelligence (AI). Whereas general-purpose clouds like Amazon and Microsoft support a broad range of tasks, CoreWeave rents access to large clusters of powerful GPUs that are primarily used for a single purpose: training and running AI models.

CoreWeave's competitive edge comes from its specialized infrastructure and expertise in managing large GPU clusters. The company routinely delivers leading results at the MLPerf benchmarks, objective tests that evaluate AI systems across training and inference tasks. In September, independent research company SemiAnalysis recognized CoreWeave as the best AI cloud for the third consecutive time.

"CoreWeave continues to set the benchmark for AI cloud performance by demonstrating strong technical execution and operational maturity in managing large-scale AI solutions," wrote Dylan Patel, chief analyst at SemiAnalysis.

CoreWeave delivered strong second-quarter financial results, with revenue soaring 112% to $2.5 billion. But the company is leaning heavily on debt to finance the infrastructure expansion needed to sustain that growth, and interest expense is weighing on profitability. In fact, interest expense rose 140% and consumed 25% of sales in the second quarter.

On the bright side, CoreWeave reported $679 million in cash from operations, up from a $251 million loss in the same quarter last year. And the stock looks rather attractive at 3.6 times sales, especially when Wall Street expects sales to grow at 130% annually through 2027.

Nebius operates a cloud computing platform purpose-built for AI. While SemiAnalysis has consistently ranked CoreWeave as the industry leader, Nebius closed the gap over the past year. CoreWeave was the only AI cloud awarded the top rating (platinum) in November 2025, but Nebius joined the platinum tier in September 2026.

SemiAnalysis explained, "While CoreWeave still sets the technical bar for others to follow, Nebius is now an established provider that consistently commands premium pricing over others." The report highlighted Nebius' large deals with hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Microsoft, as well as smaller deals with Reflection AI and Palantir Technologies.

Nebius delivered impressive financial results in the second quarter. Revenue soared 454% to $582 billion, and GAAP earnings improved to $2.05 per diluted share, up from a loss of $0.68 in the same quarter last year. Additionally, whereas CoreWeave's interest expense consumed 25% of revenue, Nebius' interest expense consumed 20% of revenue.

Nebius stock looks expensive at 31 times sales, but the valuation is a bit more tolerable in context. Wall Street estimates sales will increase at 350% annually through 2027, meaning the stock currently trades at 3.4 times projected 2027 sales. Even so, I prefer CoreWeave over Nebius given its status as the industry leader and its cheaper valuation.

Alnylam Pharmaceuticals develops RNA interference (RNAi) medications, treatments that silence specific disease-causing genes before harmful proteins are made. Its marketed therapies primarily address rare genetic disorders, and its pipeline spans treatments for cardiovascular, metabolic, and neurological diseases, often focusing on conditions with limited existing treatment options.

Alnylam reported encouraging third-quarter financial results. Product revenue increased 52% to $1.2 billion, driven by strong sales growth across its transthyretin (TTR) franchise. Amvuttra and Onpattro, treatments for a rare hereditary condition called TTR-mediated amyloidosis, accounted for about 90% of product revenue.

Looking ahead, Alnylam has an extensive product pipeline, and one of its most promising novel therapies is nucresiran, a next-generation RNAi medication designed to treat TTR-mediated amyloidosis with less frequent dosing than Amvuttra and Onpattro. Nucresiran is currently in Phase 3 clinical trials, and Alnylam anticipates a 2030 product launch with an indication for cardiomyopathy caused by TTR-mediated amyloidosis.

Alnylam currently trades at 4.3 times sales, its cheapest valuation in the past decade. That multiple looks particularly attractive because Wall Street estimates revenue will increase at 24% annually through 2027. Investors seeking greater exposure to the healthcare sector or pharmaceutical stocks should consider buying a small position in Alnylam.

Trevor Jennewine has positions in Amazon and Palantir Technologies. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Palantir Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3196. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

The company says you can then use natural language for both music-related commands and information searches. The company gives the following music examples:

As well as a couple of general knowledge examples:

Sonos says that early access to the beta is only available to customers based in the US, that numbers will be limited, and enrollment is not guaranteed. However, if you want to request access, here’s how to do so:

If accepted, access begins from Friday and you’ll find setup instructions here.

Apple gave me the OLED iPad mini of my dreams, but the budget tier dies with it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I recently called out Apple’s new “why not” era under CEO John Ternus — a chaotic, experimental chapter bringing us the $2,000 iPhone Duo and $3,000 touchscreen MacBook Pros. Well, the iPad mini 8 just arrived, and it perfectly encapsulates the dark side of this new philosophy.

I just finished reading Tony Polanco’s review of the new mini, and I completely agree with his assessment: it is a stunning piece of hardware. That new OLED panel is a visual marvel, the IP67 water resistance is a massive structural win, and it is undeniably one of the most capable tablets Apple has ever made.

And then, I looked at the pricing ladder, and realized it revealed something grave. The iPad mini 8 is proof that Apple’s “budget” tier is officially dead, replaced by sneaky paywalls, binned silicon and a display refresh rate that would have been considered “old” back in 2018.

By stuffing flagship features into a smaller chassis, compromising weirdly in some areas and passing the skyrocketing component costs directly to you, the message is clear: buying into the Apple ecosystem today comes with a pro tax.

If the $699 starting price wasn’t concerningly high enough, Apple has incorporated tantalizing silicon upgrades into its price ladder.

In all the marketing, the Cupertino crew boasts that the new mini is powered by the 2nm A20 Pro chip from the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and Duo. But what you don’t see until you actually head to the shop is that if you buy the base model, you aren’t actually getting the full chip. You are getting a slightly nerfed version.

In fact, if you take a closer look at the specs (5-core CPU, 7-core GPU and 16-core Neural Engine vs the 6-core CPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine), something struck me. This sounds like the difference between the A18 and A18 Pro of last year — knocking a core off.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The entry-level and mid-tier models are locked to this binned option. If you want the actual A20 Pro, you’re forced to drop $1,000 on the 512GB version.

Now, is this something most people are going to feel? No. But it’s something worth noting. Apple is holding the true A20 Pro performance behind a massive storage paywall. You’re paying MacBook Air to get the real thing.

Many folks at this point will immediately point to the supply chain, and that’s fair enough. We are in the middle of a brutal global memory shortage driven by the AI data center bubble — Ternus himself said it’s “unprecedented” in Apple’s most recent earnings call, and the A20 Pro requires RAM overhead to run Apple Intelligence.

But the solution to this component inflation is rather telling. It’s something I’ve talked about with the MacBook PROLED and Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20. I’m gonna call it the OLED facade.

Rather than eating a margin hit to protect entry-level consumers, or finding a way to build a highly capable device with slightly older silicon, Apple’s gone the luxury route — packing an OLED screen into a re-engineered body and jacking up the price.

As David Naranjo, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, told me when we predicted the price of the new MacBook Pros, OLED is “becoming a way for PC makers to justify higher prices as memory and component costs go up.” Companies are “using these premium displays to protect their profits and balance the rising costs."

They aren’t just adjusting for inflation; the idea of an accessible budget-friendly tablet is slowly but surely being abandoned.

But what I find most frustrating reading Tony’s review is what Apple’s left out here.

If you’re going to lure people in with the $699 tablet, and FOMO upsell them to the fully unbinned processor and enough storage, the device needs to be a flawless flagship experience. Yet, despite the price hike, Apple still locked the display to a 60Hz refresh rate.

And despite moving the front-facing camera to the landscape edge (giving more room around the side of the camera for extra tech), there’s no Face ID.

Why? Well, I can only theorize, and that’s where I take you back to the product ladder of the iPads. If we got an iPad mini 8 with 120Hz ProMotion and Face ID, that would nerf the larger, more expensive iPad Pro. It feels hamstrung to protect that pathway to one of its $1,300+ flagships.

The iPad mini 8 is a brilliant, powerful and gorgeous device, which is why I felt so conflicted writing this. For most folks buying this, you’re going to have a great time. But it does represent an Apple that is moving away from affordability (along with the wider tech industry).

Consumers didn’t necessarily need a mini tablet capable of running a dual neural engine with an OLED panel. But in the same vein, they feel necessary in Apple’s “why not” era of building premium, experimental hardware.

John Ternus’s vision for the future is coming into focus fast, and you better start saving up because the entry-level Apple experience is quickly vanishing in the rearview mirror.

#3194. Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

#3193. Coca-Cola vs. PepsiCo: Pepsi's Revenue Dwarfs Coke's, but This Is the Number to Watch

PepsiCo's revenue runs nearly double Coca-Cola's, but Coca-Cola's steadier quarterly progression may signal stronger pricing power and operational discipline.

Coca-Cola (KO -1.07%) earns its revenue by selling nonalcoholic soft drinks, concentrates, and syrups to independent bottling partners.

During the most recent period, it concluded an operational review to formally select new agency partners tasked with managing its data and marketing operations, and it partnered with hospitality resorts to provide branded consumer experiences. A law firm also announced a formal legal investigation into a reported data breach.

PepsiCo (PEP -2.24%) earns its revenue by creating and supplying a global catalog of concentrated beverage syrups and packaged snack foods.

During the same time frame, it reached an 11-year operational agreement to formally extend its status as the exclusive beverage provider for Taco Bell, and it elected a new independent director to its board while simultaneously closing multiple regional manufacturing and warehouse facilities, resulting in localized workforce reductions.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item, and it helps independent investors measure total consumer demand before counting any underlying business expenses.

Coca-Cola vs. PepsiCo Revenue over the last 8 quarters. Note: for Q4 2025, the two companies' reporting periods differ in length by more than 14 days due to differing fiscal calendars, which can make the change between quarters look bigger or smaller than an apples-to-apples comparison would show.

Data source: Financial Modeling Prep. Note: for Q4 2025, the two companies' reporting periods differ in length by more than 14 days due to differing fiscal calendars, which can make the change between quarters look bigger or smaller than an apples-to-apples comparison would show. Data as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Coca-Cola stock has returned more than 40% in 2026 as it continues to report strong business fundamentals. Renewed investor focus on consumer staples has also boosted the stock, though the same can't be said of PepsiCo, which is essentially flat year to date.

The graph above clearly illustrates Pepsi's larger absolute revenue, but that alone hasn't been enough to juice the stock this year. In its latest earnings release on Oct. 8, the company cut its 2026 core EPS outlook to 1% to 2% growth as North American beverage volumes fell modestly in the quarter. A week later, KFC confirmed it was switching from providing Pepsi to Coke products in its more than 3,700 U.S. restaurants by spring 2027. According to BofA, the account is worth about $500 million in annual sales. But beyond the roughly 3% hit to Pepsi's sales, it raises the possibility of other large accounts following suit. Earlier this year, Marriott announced it was replacing PepsiCo with Coca-Cola as its exclusive global beverage provider.

Those large accounts can move the revenue needle, but investors should also pay attention to operating margin, which measures the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after paying for the cost of goods sold (COGS) and regular operating expenses. Coca-Cola's operating margin was 33.4% in Q3, up from 32% last year. In contrast, PepsiCo's Q3 operating margin was 16.9%, an improvement over last year's 14.9%.

That difference is because Coca-Cola's business model is much more asset-light than PepsiCo's. It primarily makes and sells syrups and drink concentrates to independent bottling partners, avoiding the capital investment involved with things like building and managing factories and maintaining delivery fleets. That business model has served Coke well for years, and should allow the company to navigate macroeconomic pressures more easily.

If a school doesn't want AI in search, it doesn't get search at all

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each school can do what it wants when it comes to restricting or banning AI. However, a new report from The New York Times report found that schools that completely ban AI will also lose access to Google Search, one of the most ubiquitous tools on the internet for finding, well, anything.

"Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. He also explained that students "will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available."

Getting through college without access to Google sounds difficult, since almost everyone goes there when they need to learn something. Sure, Google alternatives exist, but for most people, an online search is still called "Googling."

As you might expect, Google's stance has drawn pushback. Lina Khan, former chair of the FTC, said to the NYT that Google is using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its AI.

Obviously, Google is justifying this move by saying that AI is an integrated part of search as it stands now. And that might be true, but we had many, many years of Google Search without AI, so it's certainly possible to find content on the web without it.

"This latest move shows it remains unchastened. As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools," Khan added. "Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line."

Two options for search inside school-issued accounts will launch in early 2027.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The first option will be search with AI overviews and AI chats, similar to the experience we use every day. The other will be search with Guided Learning, the student feature within Google’s Gemini chatbot. This feature is meant to guide students step-by-step without just giving them the answers. It is supposed to offer an experience similar to one-on-one tutoring.

Either way, we know it's possible to use search without AI, and if Google really wanted to, it could almost certainly allow schools to keep using its search engine without AI. We did it for years.

Will Google stick to its guns here, or will the company back down if there's enough backlash? After all, Google makes a lot of its money from search ads, and if It suddenly lost millions of students, that could hurt the bottom line over time.

#3189. Goldman Sachs Research Expects Slower S&P 500 Earnings Growth in 2027 (Only 18%). Can the Bull Market Keep Going?

S&P 500 earnings growth might slow in 2027. That doesn't mean investors should stop buying stocks.

Amid signs of rising risk facing tech stocks and the artificial intelligence (AI) sector, new research from Goldman Sachs (GS -0.29%) is cautiously optimistic about the S&P 500 index (^GSPC +0.36%).

According to Bloomberg reporting as of Oct. 26, Goldman Sachs expects S&P 500 earnings growth to drop from 29% in 2026 to 18% in 2027. But that strong growth could still be bullish for another good year of S&P 500 returns in 2027. Goldman analyst Tony Pasquariello wrote that "The bull market should live on, but it will pack less punch and be messier along the way."

Let's look at why Goldman Sachs' analysis might be a hopeful sign for your investments -- even if there are some big risks and doubts facing the S&P 500.

The S&P 500 has delivered a solid return of about 11% year to date, as of Nov. 3. But there are signs of possible trouble ahead.

During the past few weeks since reaching a new all-time high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 has declined by about 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index is down by about 8% in that time. Investors seem to be worrying that major tech companies are spending too much on AI data centers and developing expensive models, while (so far) showing limited signs of profitable new AI products for the hyperscalers or meaningful AI productivity gains in the wider economy.

If the high hopes of AI investors fail to materialize, that could be bad news for the stock market. But if the wider S&P 500 beyond the AI hyperscalers can keep delivering strong earnings growth in 2027, that could prolong the bull market.

It appears that, for now, there is sound earnings growth happening across the S&P 500, not just in the AI-related tech companies. According to FactSet's Oct. 30 update on S&P 500 earnings season: "All eleven sectors are reporting year-over-year earnings growth. Seven of these sectors are reporting double-digit growth, led by the Energy, Information Technology, and Materials sectors."

Does this mean that the rest of the S&P 500 is safe from a possible AI downturn? Maybe not. Goldman Sachs research on Sept. 23 calculated that almost half of S&P 500 earnings-per-share (EPS) growth in 2026 came from AI investment by hyperscalers (about $800 billion in 2026). If the AI boom falters, or if major tech companies stop spending so much on AI capital expenditures, that would likely have a negative impact on S&P 500 share prices in the short term.

This has been a good year for the stock market, but there are signs of a possible slowdown ahead. How should you invest? Be prepared for more volatility, but stick to your long-term plan. Even if you're a little concerned about a possible bear market or short-term sell-off in major tech stocks, now could be a good time to buy the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +0.32%).

This exchange-traded fund (ETF) has delivered average annual returns of 15.4% during the past 10 years, and about 12% during the past five years. Even if there is a bear market in the short term in 2027, this diversified mix of the largest 500 publicly traded companies in America tends to bounce back and deliver strong gains in the long term.

No single Wall Street bank or analyst is always 100% right. But if Goldman Sachs' analysis on this topic is generally on target, this could be a good sign for another year of decent returns. Keep in mind that the long-run average annual return of the S&P 500 is about 10%. So even if 2027 is an average year, that would still be good news for investors who own S&P 500 ETFs for the long term.

‘A Dog’s Perfect Christmas’ is cozy but no Christmas classic

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix’s holiday movie slate for 2026 begins its rollout this week, starting with “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a streaming original that so rigidly sticks to the genre conventions that it is as predictable as unwrapping a Christmas present from that one relative who always gets you an Axe body spray gift set. Within seconds, you know exactly what you’re getting.

All the trappings of a family-focused festive-themed comedy-drama are here. By the end, everything is wrapped up in a neat bow, all to send viewers into the credits with a warm fuzzy feeling. It’s a safe holiday movie created in a tinsel-laden laboratory, where artistic merit is not the end goal. Instead, the objective is to create a product palatable for all ages.

But if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” proves anything, it’s that throwing a couple of cute canine companions into the mix can make even a Christmas movie this flavorless at least tolerable. Which isn’t to say it has any original musings on the special connection between household pets and their owners. It doesn’t even break from the weary formula established in other dog movies like “A Dog’s Purpose” and “A Dog’s Journey.”

However, the dogs were lovable enough to thaw out even my cynical soul. It might not be a future Christmas classic — the likes of “It’s A Wonderful Life” and “Elf” will not fear their place in any family’s annual seasonal watchlist being pinched by this new Netflix movie — but dog lovers everywhere will probably find this film cozy enough to watch, if only once.

Based on the novel by W. Bruce Cameron, author of “A Dog’s Purpose,” this movie focuses on the Goss family. Their holiday festivities are already off to a rocky start, with grandpa Sander (Dennis Quaid) grieving the loss of his wife two years prior, husband Hunter (Milo Ventimiglia) putting work first, and mother Juliana (Kathleen Rose Perkins) struggling to find common ground with her moody teenage daughter, Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson).

Things take a further turn when a medical emergency throws the family into turmoil and threatens to bring a swift end to any lingering holiday cheer. It’s up to the Goss' wise old dog, a basset hound named Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), and an energetic new arrival, a Corgi puppy named Ruby (Sadie Hatch), to bring the humans back together.

I really cannot overstate just how generic “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is. All its narrative beats have been seen in countless other holiday movies, and it has no desire to rework the genre trappings. But whether you demand, or particularly look for, originality in your holiday watchlist is a matter of personal preference. If you want a cozy family comedy, it’s a suitable way to spend 100 minutes, and it'll probably make for great background noise while putting up your own seasonal decorations, if that's your thing.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Another notable area where “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” comes up short is in its insistence on over-explaining. It’s been suggested that Netflix has a mandate that its movies need to reiterate key plot points for viewers only half-watching, and while the streamer denies this, “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is evidence to the contrary. Characters often speak unnaturally, regurgitating facts as if they know a third party is watching their holiday season unfold and might need a reminder (or three) to follow along.

But even if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” will no doubt be forgotten long before you take down your tree and household decorations for another year, in the moment, it’s by no means offensively bad. It’s just bland. But above all, the two dogs at the heart of the holiday crowd-pleaser are very cute and given enough screen time to make their presence felt.

“A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” celebrates family, especially these four-legged members of our homes who are just as important to the unit as any human. That’s a message that dog owners everywhere will relate to, and it gives this Netflix movie a crowd-pleasing quality. I guess it really does prove that the inclusion of a dog (or two) can make anything watchable.

#3187. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."
